text: Qdrant stores each collection as a set of immutable segments. New points are written to a write-ahead log and an in-memory segment, then flushed to disk and indexed with HNSW. A background optimizer merges small segments, which keeps search latency stable as the corpus grows. Payload indexes can be created for metadata fields used in filters, so a filtered vector search does not scan every point in the collection.

Scalar quantization maps float32 vector components to int8 integers, reducing memory by roughly four times. Qdrant stores the quantized vectors in RAM, retrieves a larger candidate set, and then rescores those candidates with the original vectors. The rescoring step recovers most of the accuracy loss. Product quantization compresses further but is better suited to corpora of hundreds of millions of vectors where memory is the binding constraint.

HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph. The parameter m controls how many neighbours each node keeps and therefore memory use and recall. ef_construct controls how many candidates are examined while inserting a point, trading index build time for graph quality. The search-time parameter ef controls the candidate list size: higher ef improves recall at the cost of latency. A common starting point is m=16, ef_construct=128 and ef between 64 and 128.

Chunking decides what a single embedding represents. Fixed-size character windows are simple and predictable, but splitting mid-sentence loses meaning, so boundaries should snap to whitespace or paragraph marks. Overlapping windows preserve context that straddles a boundary at the cost of duplicate storage. For technical documentation, chunks of 600 to 1000 characters with 10 to 20 percent overlap are a practical default. Headings and document identifiers belong in the payload so retrieval can filter and cite them.

Retrieval quality must be measured against a labelled query set. Recall at k reports the share of expected documents that appear in the top k results. Mean reciprocal rank reports how early the first relevant document appears. Both metrics should be tracked whenever the embedding model, chunk size or index parameters change. A pipeline that cannot report a retrieval metric cannot tell an improvement from a regression.

Embedding dimension determines vector size and therefore storage and search cost. A 384-dimensional float32 vector occupies about 1.5 kilobytes before payload, so ten million chunks need roughly 15 gigabytes of raw vector storage. Quantization to int8 cuts that to under 4 gigabytes. Larger models such as 1024-dimensional multilingual encoders improve semantic matching but multiply both memory and inference cost, which is why dimension is a capacity decision as much as a quality decision.

Oracle Cloud block volumes are network-attached disks that can be detached from one instance and attached to another in the same availability domain. They support online resizing and policy-based backups. For a vector database, the volume holds segments, the write-ahead log and snapshots, so it must be sized for the corpus plus index overhead and at least one full snapshot. Attaching the volume at a stable mount point keeps the compose bind mounts unchanged across instance replacement.

Ampere A1 Flex shapes provide up to four OCPUs and 24 gigabytes of memory inside the Oracle Always Free allowance, split across any number of instances. For a vector workload the memory-to-core ratio matters more than raw CPU: HNSW graph traversal is memory-bound, while embedding generation is CPU-bound. A common split is one instance for Qdrant with the larger memory share and a second instance, or a container with a CPU quota, for embedding workers.

Qdrant snapshots capture a collection at a point in time and can be restored into a different collection or cluster. Snapshot creation streams segment data to the snapshots directory, so that directory should live on the persistent volume rather than the container filesystem. A restore test is part of the backup policy: an untested snapshot is an assumption, not a recovery plan.

Idempotent ingestion makes re-runs safe. Deriving point identifiers deterministically from the document identifier and chunk index means a repeated run overwrites the same points instead of appending duplicates. Upserts should be batched to amortise network and index overhead, and the worker should log the number of points written versus the collection count so an operator can confirm the corpus landed exactly once.
